source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. V (Montreuil)

1.title: Expositio capituli primi: In diebus Assueri regis
1.title_en: Exposition of the first chapter: In the days of king Assuerus

paras.t: Liber Esther inter Scripturas computatur canonicas, atque in ordine Hagiographorum reponitur. Accidit quoque historia ista post reditum filiorum Israel a Babylonica captivitate: et primo isto narratur capitulo, qualiter Assuerus rex suam repudiavit uxorem; secundo, qualiter puellam nomine Esther, natione Hebræam, duxit in conjugem: deinde qualiter per eamdem procurata sit liberatio Judæorum a mortis periculo.
paras.en: The book of Esther is counted among the canonical Scriptures, and is placed in the order of the Hagiographa [the third part of the Hebrew Bible, after the Law and the Prophets]. This history took place after the return of the children of Israel from the Babylonian captivity; and in this first chapter it is told how King Assuerus put away his wife; in the second, how he took to wife a maiden named Esther, a Hebrew by birth; and then how through her the deliverance of the Jews from the danger of death was brought about.

paras.t: In diebus Assueri, qui regnavit ab India usque Æthiopiam super centum viginti septem provincias. Assuerus iste rex fuit Persarum atque Medorum: quem aliqui dicunt fuisse octavum post Cyrum regem, qui monarchiam obtinuit, omissis duobus magis, id est sapientibus, qui post Cambysem filium Cyri regis regnasse dicuntur septem mensibus tantum, ut quidam hic scribit. Quod non apparet idonee dictum, quia (ut Magister in historiis narrat) primus illorum duorum sapientium regnavit mensibus septem, et post eum frater ipsius modico tempore, ita quod duratio regnationis eorum non se extendebat ad annum unum. Hujus opinionis, quod scilicet Assuerus fuit octavus post Cyrum, fuit auctor Scholasticæ historiæ, dicens quod post duos magos illos regnavit Darius filius Hystaspis, unus septem sapientium seu magorum, qui post regem judicabant et administrabant regnum Persarum; post Darium, filius ejus Xerxes, post quem, filius ejus Artaxerxes: post hunc, filius ejus Xerxes secundus, cui successit Sogdianus, et Sogdiano Darius cognomento Nothus, huicque Dario Artaxerxes, alio nomine Assuerus, sub quo contigit historia Esther. Alii dicunt, quod Assuerus iste fuit quartus post Cyrum: quod Josephus sensisse videtur undecimo libro Antiquitatum, affirmans post Cyrum regnasse filium ejus Cambysem: post Cambysem, Darium filium Hystaspis, qui Darius non fuit de semine Cambysis; post Darium autem, filium ejus Xerxem; post Xerxem, filium ejus Artaxerxem. Quidam vero opinantur, quod Assuerus iste successit immediate Cyro regi Persarum, vel saltem Cambysi filio Cyri.
paras.en: [[1:1|In the days of Assuerus, who reigned from India to Ethiopia over a hundred and twenty seven provinces|In diebus Assueri, qui regnavit ab India usque Æthiopiam super centum viginti septem provincias]]. This Assuerus was king of the Persians and Medes; and some say that he was the eighth after King Cyrus, who obtained the monarchy, leaving out the two magi, that is, wise men, who are said to have reigned after Cambyses son of King Cyrus for seven months only, as a certain writer has it here. This does not seem well said, for (as the Master tells in the Histories) the first of those two wise men reigned seven months, and after him his brother a short time, so that the length of their reign did not reach a year. The author of the Scholastic History was of this opinion, namely that Assuerus was the eighth after Cyrus: he says that after those two magi reigned Darius the son of Hystaspes, one of the seven wise men or magi who after the king judged and administered the kingdom of the Persians; after Darius his son Xerxes; after him his son Artaxerxes; after him his son Xerxes the Second, whom Sogdianus succeeded; Sogdianus was succeeded by Darius surnamed Nothus, and this Darius by Artaxerxes, by another name Assuerus, under whom the history of Esther took place. Others say that this Assuerus was the fourth after Cyrus, which Josephus seems to have held in the eleventh book of the Antiquities, where he affirms that after Cyrus reigned his son Cambyses; after Cambyses, Darius the son of Hystaspes, which Darius was not of the seed of Cambyses; after Darius his son Xerxes; after Xerxes his son Artaxerxes. Others again think that this Assuerus succeeded Cyrus king of the Persians immediately, or at least Cambyses the son of Cyrus.

paras.t: Præterea Nicolaus de Lyra positiones has recitans, dicit quod tertia verisimilior videatur; et addit, quod Rabbi Salomon uno loco dicit Assuerum hunc immediate Cyro successisse, et tamen super Danielem tenet, quod Cambyses fuit medius rex inter ipsos. Ratio autem quæ movit Lyram ad reprobandum duas primas positiones est, quoniam præsupposuit, quod Mardochæus captus fuit cum Jechonia rege Juda: quod infra dicit patere. Sicque per durationem Babylonicæ captivitatis, et per tempora quibus præfati reges Persarum regnaverunt, probat quod Mardochæus primo anno regni Assueri fuit ad minus ducentorum quinque annorum, et adhuc alii multi anni essent addendi. Non est autem probabile, quod tam diu vixerit, aut in tanta ætate facere potuisset quæ legitur infra fecisse. Secundam quoque positionem redarguit, quia secundum eam Mardochæus in principio regni Assueri fuisset centum quinquaginta sex annorum, imo et plurium. Itaque tertiam sequens positionem, dicit quod Mardochæus in principio regni Assueri fuit circiter centum annorum.
paras.en: Further, Nicholas of Lyra, reciting these positions, says that the third seems the more likely; and he adds that Rabbi Solomon in one place says that this Assuerus succeeded Cyrus immediately, and yet on Daniel holds that Cambyses was a king between them. The reason that moved Lyra to reject the first two positions is that he presupposed that Mardochai was taken captive with Jechonias king of Juda, which he says is plain below[[Esth 2:6||]] [the margin's reference here is misread; the passage is Esth 2:6]. And so, from the length of the Babylonian captivity and from the times in which the aforesaid kings of the Persians reigned, he proves that in the first year of the reign of Assuerus Mardochai was at least two hundred and five years old, and many more years would still have to be added. Now it is not probable that he lived so long, or that at so great an age he could have done what we read below that he did. He refutes the second position too, because according to it Mardochai at the beginning of the reign of Assuerus would have been a hundred and fifty-six years old, or even more. So, following the third position, he says that at the beginning of the reign of Assuerus Mardochai was about a hundred years old.

paras.t: Verum Rabbi Paulus omnia ista argumenta Lyræ conatur cassare una solutione. Lyra namque se fundat in eo quod sequenti habetur capitulo: Erat autem vir Judæus in Susis civitate, vocabulo Mardochæus, filius Jair, filii Semei, filii Cis de stirpe Jemini, qui translatus fuerat de Jerusalem, eo tempore quo Jechoniam regem Juda Nabuchodonosor rex Babylonis transtulerat. In hac auctoritate hoc relativum, Qui, Lyra refert ad Mardochæum, quod Rabbi Paulus dicit posse referri ad Cis proavum Mardochæi: velut si dicamus, David fuit filius Jesse filii Obed filii Booz, qui contraxit cum Ruth Moabitide, relativum hoc, Qui, refertur ad Booz, non ad David. Verumtamen ista solutio Rabbi Pauli non invenitur idonea. Quamvis enim quod ait de relatione relativi, possit salvari, sumendo præinducta verba secundum se, tamen si attendantur verba sequentia, veritatem non habent, quia secundo capitulo post præallegata verba immediate subjungitur, Qui fuit nutricius filiæ fratris sui Edissæ, qui altero nomine Esther vocabatur. Quo constat, quod utrumque hoc relativum, Qui, seu unum repetitum, ad Mardochæum sit referendum.
paras.en: But Rabbi Paul [Paul of Burgos, in his Additions to Lyra] tries to undo all these arguments of Lyra with one answer. For Lyra founds himself on what is had in the following chapter: [[Esth 2:5|There was a man in the city of Susan, a Jew, named Mardochai, the son of Jair, the son of Semei, the son of Cis, of the race of Jemini|Erat autem vir Judæus in Susis civitate, vocabulo Mardochæus, filius Jair, filii Semei, filii Cis de stirpe Jemini]], [[Esth 2:6|Who had been carried away from Jerusalem at the time that Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon carried away Jechonias king of Juda|qui translatus fuerat de Jerusalem, eo tempore quo Jechoniam regem Juda Nabuchodonosor rex Babylonis transtulerat]]. In this text Lyra refers the relative *Who* to Mardochai, while Rabbi Paul says that it can be referred to Cis, the great-grandfather of Mardochai: as if we say, David was the son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Booz, who married Ruth the Moabitess, the relative *who* is referred to Booz, not to David. But this answer of Rabbi Paul is not found sound. For although what he says of the reference of the relative could be saved by taking the words quoted by themselves, yet if the following words are attended to, it does not hold true; for in the second chapter, straight after the words quoted, there is added: [[Esth 2:7|And he had brought up his brother's daughter Edissa, who by another name was called Esther|Qui fuit nutricius filiæ fratris sui Edissæ, qui altero nomine Esther vocabatur]]. From this it is clear that both relatives, *who*, or the one relative repeated, must be referred to Mardochai.

paras.t: Sed his obviare videtur quod Magister in historiis refert: Erat tunc in Susis Judæus vocabulo Mardochæus de tribu Jemini, qui descenderat de transmigratione Jechoniæ: hic erat nutricius Esther. Ex quibus verbis apparet, quod per nativitatem descenderit de aliquo transmigrato cum Jechonia, præsertim quum glossa ejusdem historiæ dicat, Descenderat de transmigratione non immediate, sed per successiones, quia pater ejus vel avus vel proavus descenderat. Ad quod dicendum, quod in Scholastica historia in libro correspondente quarto Regum, manifeste habetur, quod Nabuchodonosor transtulit cum Joachin seu Jechonia in summa quasi decem millia, inter quos erant Mardochæus et Ezechiel. Et sic magis standum videtur textui, quam glossæ illius, et præsertim textui libri hujus canonici.
paras.en: But what the Master relates in the Histories seems to stand against this: There was at that time in Susan a Jew named Mardochai, of the tribe of Jemini, who was descended from the transmigration of Jechonias; he was the foster-father of Esther. From these words it appears that by birth he was descended from someone carried away with Jechonias, especially since the gloss on that same History says: He was descended from the transmigration not immediately, but by succession, because his father or grandfather or great-grandfather had been carried away. To this it must be said that in the Scholastic History, in the book corresponding to the fourth of Kings, it is plainly stated that Nabuchodonosor carried away with Joachin or Jechonias about ten thousand in all[[4 Kings 24:14||]] [the margin gives IV Reg. xxiv], among whom were Mardochai and Ezechiel. And so it seems better to stand by the text than by its gloss, and above all by the text of this canonical book.

paras.t: Itaque veriorem puto primam positionem, quam Magister in historiis sequitur, et quod Josephus aliquos omisit. Nam secundus Xerxes quem omisit, regnavit duobus mensibus: Sogdianus vero quem omisit, mensibus septem. Quid autem de Mardochæo senserit Josephus, in libro Antiquitatum non reperi, nisi quod undecimo libro Antiquitatum narrat Darium regem scripsisse Samaritis: Zorobabel et Ananias et Mardochæus legati Judæorum vos accusant. Quod tamen de isto Mardochæo non arbitror dictum, sed de alio quodam ad Judæam a Babylone reverso: ad quam Judæam Mardochæus non rediit, nisi forsan dicatur ad tempus rediisse, et rursus in Babylonem reversus. Verum juxta hæc, remanet quæstio, qualiter potuerit Mardochæus tam diu vixisse, et in senectute tam magna egisse quæ infra de eo narrantur. Ad quod faciliter poterit responderi, si ad omnipotentiam Dei respiciatur, qui per Mardochæum voluit Israelitico populo subvenire. Imo infra tempus evangelicæ legis leguntur quidam vixisse usque ad quadringentos annos, sicut in Chronicis Martini recitatur de quodam, qui ob senium vocabatur Joannes de Tempore. Et nuper fuit in ducatu Hollandiæ quidam, qui supra centum multis annis vixisse asseritur. Tamen de his qui infra certitudinem sunt, non convenit multum assertorie loqui.
paras.en: So I think the first position the truer, the one the Master follows in the Histories, and that Josephus left some kings out. For the second Xerxes, whom he left out, reigned two months, and Sogdianus, whom he left out, seven months. What Josephus thought of Mardochai I have not found in the book of the Antiquities, except that in the eleventh book of the Antiquities he tells that King Darius wrote to the Samaritans: Zorobabel and Ananias and Mardochai, the envoys of the Jews, accuse you. Yet I do not think this was said of this Mardochai, but of some other who returned from Babylon to Judea; to which Judea Mardochai did not return, unless perhaps it is said that he returned for a time and went back again to Babylon. But on this view the question remains how Mardochai could have lived so long, and in old age have done the great things that are told of him below [the margin refers to the later chapters of Esther; its reading is unclear]. This can easily be answered if we look to the omnipotence of God, who willed to help the Israelite people through Mardochai. Indeed, even within the time of the law of the Gospel some are read to have lived up to four hundred years, as is told in the Chronicles of Martin of one who for his great age was called John of the Times. And lately there was a man in the duchy of Holland who is said to have lived many years beyond a hundred. Yet of things that fall short of certainty it is not fitting to speak too assertively.

paras.t: Itaque, In diebus Assueri, quando sedit in solio, id est regio throno, regni sui, tanquam receptus et roboratus, Susa civitas regni Persarum, regni ejus exordium fuit, id est caput atque metropolis. Tertio ergo anno imperii sui fecit grande convivium cunctis principibus et pueris suis, id est ministris, fortissimis Persarum, et Medorum inclytis, ac præfectis provinciarum coram se, ut ostenderet divitias gloriæ regni sui, centum et octoginta diebus. Circa hoc dicit quidam, non esse verisimile quod homines, præsertim qui a remotis venerunt, tot diebus vacaverint: ideo dicit, hos centum octoginta dies esse referendos ad tempus præparationis convivii: nec exhibuisse regem populo suo, nisi convivium septem dierum, de quo subditur: Quumque implerentur dies convivii, invitavit omnem populum qui inventus est in Susis, a maximo usque ad minimum, et septem diebus jussit convivium præparari in vestibulo horti et nemoris.
paras.en: So then, in the days of Assuerus, [[1:2|When he sat on the throne|quando sedit in solio]], that is, the royal seat, [[1:2|of his kingdom|regni sui]], as one received and established, [[1:2|the city Susan|Susa civitas]] of the kingdom of the Persians [[1:2|was the capital of his kingdom|regni ejus exordium fuit]] [*exordium*, literally “beginning”], that is, its head and metropolis. [[1:3|Now in the third year of his reign he made a great feast for all the princes, and for his servants|Tertio ergo anno imperii sui fecit grande convivium cunctis principibus et pueris suis]], that is, his ministers, [[1:3|for the most mighty of the Persians, and the nobles of the Medes, and the governors of the provinces in his sight|fortissimis Persarum, et Medorum inclytis, ac præfectis provinciarum coram se]], [[1:4|That he might shew the riches of the glory of his kingdom|ut ostenderet divitias gloriæ regni sui]], [[1:4|for a hundred and fourscore days|centum et octoginta diebus]]. On this a certain writer says that it is not likely that men, especially those who came from far, should have been free for so many days; and so he says that these hundred and eighty days are to be referred to the time of preparing the feast, and that the king gave his people only the feast of seven days, of which it is added: [[1:5|And when the days of the feast were expired, he invited all the people that were found in Susan, from the greatest to the least|Quumque implerentur dies convivii, invitavit omnem populum qui inventus est in Susis, a maximo usque ad minimum]]: [[1:5|and commanded a feast to be made seven days in the court of the garden, and of the wood|et septem diebus jussit convivium præparari in vestibulo horti et nemoris]].

paras.t: Sed istud ineptissime dictum censeo, præsertim quum nec auctoritate, nec idonea ratione probetur, et textus manifeste dicat oppositum. Nec mirum, quod ad instantiam tanti regis vacaverint tot diebus, quum interim gratis lautissime reficerentur. Nec verum est, nec ullam apparentiam habet, quod præparatio convivii duraverit centum octoginta diebus, quum omnia necessaria haberentur copiose, imo copiosissime ad manum, quum in textu dicatur, quod exhibuit istud convivium, ut ostenderet divitias regni sui. Insuper, textus evidenter inter convivia ista distinguit, tam quoad locum, quam quantum ad tempus, et item quantum ad invitatos. De primo namque convivio ait, Fecit grande convivium multo tempore, scilicet centum et octoginta diebus; nec fit mentio ibi de speciali loco. Deinde tractat de convivio septem dierum. Nec in descriptione primi convivii ulla fit mentio de præparatione convivii, sed de exhibitione dumtaxat. Imo in descriptione convivii septem dierum fit verbum de præparatione convivii, et nihilo minus exponitur hoc de convivii exhibitione: ergo potius primum. Rursus, descripto primo convivio, adjungitur, Quumque implerentur dies convivii; et consequenter tractat de secundo convivio, quod affirmat septem durasse diebus. Iterum, primum convivium asserit factum cunctis principibus et pueris regis, fortissimis Persarum, et Medorum inclytis, et præfectis provinciarum. Secundum vero convivium asserit factum omni populo in civitate Susis invento. Et hæc omnia etiam Josephus libro Antiquitatum undecimo protestatur: qui etiam scribit, quod rex misit per omnes provincias, denuntians ut opera relinquerent, et multis diebus pro ejus imperio lætarentur: quo patet, quod diu vacabant. Quibus concordat omnino Scholastica historia, quæ fatetur primum convivium factum esse in domo illa mirabili, de qua legitur in historia Alexandri, cujus columnæ erant argenteæ, tectum instar firmamenti concameratum, habens gemmas diversicolores in figuram siderum et signorum dispositas. De hoc narrat et Josephus: Tabernaculum fixerat rex aureis argenteisque columnis, vela purpurea super eas extendens, ut multa millia discumbentium operirent.
paras.en: But I judge this most unfittingly said, especially since it is proved neither by authority nor by sound reason, and the text plainly says the opposite. Nor is it any wonder that at the bidding of so great a king they were free for so many days, since meanwhile they were most sumptuously feasted for nothing. Nor is it true, nor has it any likelihood, that the preparation of the feast lasted a hundred and eighty days, since everything needed was at hand in plenty, indeed in the greatest plenty, as the text says that he gave this feast [[1:4|That he might shew the riches|ut ostenderet divitias]] of his kingdom. Moreover, the text clearly distinguishes between these feasts, as to place, as to time, and also as to the guests. For of the first feast it says: [[1:3|he made a great feast|Fecit grande convivium]] [[1:4|for a long time|multo tempore]], namely [[1:4|for a hundred and fourscore days|centum et octoginta diebus]]; and no special place is mentioned there. Then it treats of the feast of seven days. Nor in the description of the first feast is any mention made of the preparing of the feast, but only of the giving of it; whereas in the description of the feast of seven days a word is said of the preparing of the feast, and none the less this is explained of the giving of the feast: all the more, then, the first. Again, when the first feast has been described, it is added: [[1:5|And when the days of the feast were expired|Quumque implerentur dies convivii]]; and then it treats of the second feast, which it affirms lasted seven days. Again, it asserts that the first feast was made for all the princes and servants of the king, the mightiest of the Persians, the nobles of the Medes, and the governors of the provinces; but that the second feast was made for all the people found in the city of Susan. And Josephus too bears witness to all this in the eleventh book of the Antiquities; he also writes that the king sent through all the provinces, bidding them leave their work and make merry for many days at his command: from which it is plain that they were free for a long time. With this the Scholastic History wholly agrees, which says that the first feast was made in that wonderful house of which we read in the history of Alexander, whose pillars were of silver, and whose roof was vaulted like the firmament, with gems of different colours set in the shapes of the stars and the signs. Josephus too tells of this: The king had pitched a tent on pillars of gold and silver, spreading purple veils over them, so as to cover many thousands of guests.

paras.t: Secundum autem convivium, juxta prætacta, factum est in vestibulo horti et nemoris, id est pomœrii nemorosi, quod regio cultu et manu, id est regali ornatu ac artificio, consitum fuit, id est consertum ac decoratum aromaticis fructiferisque arboribus, prout tanti imperatoris decuit claritatem. De hoc in Historiis legitur: Post hos centum octoginta dies invitavit omnem populum qui erat in Susis, et discubuerunt extra domum septem diebus in vestibulo horti deliciarum: in quo fuit vinea habens stipites argenteos, palmites aureos, et botros ex varietate gemmarum distinctos. Et pendebant ex omni parte tentoria aerii, id est albi et clari, et carbasini, id est aurei, et hyacinthini, id est cœlestis coloris: color enim hyacinthi similis perhibetur dispositioni cœlestis orbis seu sphæræ cœlestis: sustentata funibus byssinis et purpureis, id est extensa funibus factis de bysso seu candidissimo lino et de purpura, qui eburneis circulis inserti erant, id est circulis factis de ebore, quod satis forte fuit ad onus illud, et columnis marmoreis, utpote de marmore lapide factis, fulciebantur, id est, sustentabantur ex parte utraque. Lectuli quoque aurei et argentei dispositi erant, id est loca ad sedendum instar lectulorum mollia, atque operta tincturis et mixturis ex auro et argento formatis, super pavimentum vestibuli smaragdino et Pario stratum lapide, id est complanatum lapidibus de insula Paro, et similibus in colore seu dispositione gemmæ quæ smaragdus vocatur, quod mira varietate pictura decorabat.
paras.en: The second feast, as was touched on before, was made [[1:5|in the court of the garden, and of the wood|in vestibulo horti et nemoris]], that is, of a wooded orchard, [[1:5|which was planted by the care and the hand of the king|quod regio cultu et manu, id est regali ornatu ac artificio, consitum fuit]] (by the hand, that is, with royal adornment and art), that is, set close and adorned with fragrant and fruit-bearing trees, as befitted the splendour of so great an emperor. Of this we read in the Histories: After these hundred and eighty days he invited all the people that were in Susan, and they sat at table outside the house for seven days in the court of the garden of delights, in which there was a vine with stems of silver, branches of gold, and clusters marked out with a variety of gems. [[1:6|And there were hung up on every side sky coloured|Et pendebant ex omni parte tentoria aerii]] [*aerii*, Denis glosses “white and bright”], that is, white and bright, [[1:6|and green|et carbasini]] [Denis glosses *carbasini* “golden”], that is, golden, [[1:6|and violet hangings|et hyacinthini]], that is, of the colour of the sky: for the colour of the hyacinth is said to be like the look of the heavenly orb or sphere; [[1:6|fastened with cords of silk, and of purple|sustentata funibus byssinis et purpureis]], that is, stretched with cords made of byssus, or the whitest linen, and of purple, [[1:6|which were put into rings of ivory|qui eburneis circulis inserti erant]], that is, rings made of ivory, which was strong enough for that weight, [[1:6|and were held up with marble pillars|et columnis marmoreis fulciebantur]], made, that is, of marble stone; held up, that is, they were held up on both sides. [[1:6|The beds also were of gold and silver, placed in order|Lectuli quoque aurei et argentei, super pavimentum smaragdino et pario stratum lapide, dispositi erant]], that is, places for sitting, soft like little beds, and covered with dyed stuffs and blends worked with gold and silver, [[1:6|upon a floor paved with porphyry and white marble|super pavimentum vestibuli smaragdino et Pario stratum lapide]] [the Latin is *smaragdino et Pario lapide*, “emerald and Parian stone”], that is, made level with stones from the island of Paros, and with stones like in colour or look to the gem called emerald, [[1:6|which was embellished with painting of wonderful variety|quod mira varietate pictura decorabat]].

paras.t: Bibebant autem aureis poculis, id est ex vasis seu scyphis aureis; atque (ut Josephus addit) vasis illis inserti erant lapides pretiosi ad delectationem et spectaculum præparati; et aliis atque aliis vasis cibi inferebantur, id est, in vasis et scutellis ex materiis diversarum specierum aut dispositionum pretiosis, et juxta diversitatem ferculorum fuit diversitas utensilium seu vasorum. Vinum quoque, ut magnificentia regia dignum erat, abundans et præcipuum ponebatur. Nec erat qui nolentes bibere cogeret ad bibendum, importune invitando, vel ad æquales haustus hortando, ut quidam brutaliter faciunt: [quod] et in jure valde vituperatur, sanitatique mentis ac corporis adversatur; sed sicut rex statuerat, præponens mensis singulis de principibus suis, ut unusquisque quod vellet acciperet de cibo et potu cum libertate et urbanitate. Nam et naturaliter delectabile est uti libertate. Et tamen, ut Josephus refert, solitum fuit Persis cogere ad potum convivantes.
paras.en: [[1:7|drank in golden cups|Bibebant autem aureis poculis]], that is, from golden vessels or goblets; and (as Josephus adds) precious stones were set in those vessels, prepared for delight and show; [[1:7|and the meats were brought in divers vessels one after another|et aliis atque aliis vasis cibi inferebantur]], that is, in vessels and dishes precious for materials of different kinds or workmanship, and according to the variety of the courses there was a variety of utensils or vessels. [[1:7|Wine also in abundance and of the best was presented, as was worthy of a king's magnificence|Vinum quoque, ut magnificentia regia dignum erat, abundans et præcipuum ponebatur]]. [[1:8|Neither was there any one to compel them to drink that were not willing|Nec erat qui nolentes bibere cogeret ad bibendum]], by pressing invitations, or by urging them to match draught for draught, as some do like brute beasts, which is also strongly condemned in law and is contrary to the health of mind and body; [[1:8|but as the king had appointed, who set over every table one of his nobles|sed sicut rex statuerat, præponens mensis singulis de principibus suis]], [[1:8|that every man might take what he would|ut unusquisque quod vellet]] of food and drink, with freedom and courtesy. For it is naturally delightful to enjoy freedom. And yet, as Josephus relates, the Persians were accustomed to force their guests to drink.

paras.t: Vasthi quoque regina fecit convivium feminarum in palatio regis. Sicque feminæ vescebantur seorsum: quod fuit honestum, atque occasio vitandi multa peccata. Feminis quoque specialiter obest, ex virorum consortio vino repleri. Quo constat quam ineffabiliter detestabile sit, quod etiam in quibusdam urbibus Christianorum, viri et feminæ in eisdem stuphis repræsentant se nudos, et in stuphis aut balneis mulierculæ serviunt viris.
paras.en: [[1:9|Also Vasthi the queen made a feast for the women in the palace|Vasthi quoque regina fecit convivium feminarum in palatio]] of the king. And so the women ate apart, which was seemly, and a means of avoiding many sins. For it is especially harmful to women to be filled with wine in the company of men. From this it is clear how unspeakably detestable it is that even in certain cities of Christians men and women show themselves naked in the same bath-houses, and in bath-houses or baths young women wait on men.

paras.t: Itaque die septimo hujus secundi convivii, sumendo convivium pro congerie conviviorum tot dierum, quum rex esset hilarior, et post nimiam potationem incaluisset mero: vinum enim lætificat cor hominis; præcepit septem eunuchis, qui in conspectu ejus ministrabant familiarius et in mensa, ut introducerent reginam Vasthi coram rege, ut ostenderet cunctis populis et principibus adhuc ibi præsentibus, illius pulchritudinem. Erat enim pulchra valde. Quamvis enim secundum illud convivium specialiter factum sit civibus Susis, ut apparet ex littera, multi tamen ibi erant ex principibus et gentibus provinciarum regis, ut innuit Josephus: idcirco ex isto non sequitur, quod non fuit nisi unum convivium. Quæ renuit, et ad regis imperium quod per eunuchos mandaverat, venire contempsit. Hujus contrarium videtur Josephus insinuare, dicendo: Quæ pro legum Persarum custodia, prohibentium ab extraneis alienas conjugales videri, non accessit ad regem. Ex quo elicitur, quod non ex contemptu, sed potius ex pudicitia et observantia legis Persarum, prohibentis conjuges eorumdem ab alienis viris videri, non venit ad regem. Hinc aliqui dicunt in Hebræo haberi: Et renuit regina Vasthi venire secundum verbum regis in manu eunuchorum. Verum ad hoc ex verbis Josephi patet responsio. Etenim ait, quod rex sæpe misit pro ea, et tamen non acquievit: quod contemptum includebat. Rex enim in tali lege potuit dispensare.
paras.en: [[1:10|Now on the seventh day|Itaque die septimo]] of this second feast (taking *feast* for the whole series of feasts of so many days), [[1:10|when the king was merry, and after very much drinking was well warmed with wine|quum rex esset hilarior, et post nimiam potationem incaluisset mero]]: for [[Ps 103:15|wine may cheer the heart of man|vinum enim lætificat cor hominis]][[Ecclus 40:20||]] [the margin gives Ps. ciii, 15, and Ecclus. xl (?)]; [[1:10|he commanded|præcepit]] [[1:10|the seven eunuchs that served in his presence|septem eunuchis, qui in conspectu ejus ministrabant]] more familiarly and at table, [[1:11|To bring in queen Vasthi before the king|ut introducerent reginam Vasthi coram rege]], [[1:11|to shew|ut ostenderet]] [[1:11|her beauty to all the people and the princes|cunctis populis et principibus pulchritudinem illius]] who were still present there: [[1:11|for she was exceeding beautiful|Erat enim pulchra valde]]. For although that second feast was made especially for the citizens of Susan, as appears from the letter, yet many of the princes and peoples of the king's provinces were there, as Josephus hints; therefore it does not follow from this that there was only one feast. [[1:12|But she refused, and would not come at the king's commandment, which he had signified to her by the eunuchs|Quæ renuit, et ad regis imperium quod per eunuchos mandaverat, venire contempsit]] [the Latin has *venire contempsit*, “scorned to come”]. Josephus seems to hint the contrary of this, saying: She, keeping the laws of the Persians, which forbid their wives to be seen by strangers, did not come to the king. From which it is gathered that it was not out of contempt, but rather out of modesty and the keeping of the law of the Persians, which forbade their wives to be seen by other men, that she did not come to the king. Hence some say that the Hebrew has: And queen Vasthi refused to come at the word of the king by the hand of the eunuchs. But the answer to this is plain from the words of Josephus. For he says that the king sent for her often, and yet she did not consent; and this implied contempt, for the king could dispense in such a law.

paras.t: Unde iratus rex, et nimio furore succensus. Vitanda autem est regum ira, quantum rationabiliter fieri potest: quia ut in Proverbiis Salomon loquitur, Sicut fremitus leonis, ita et ira regis; qui provocat eum, peccat in animam suam. Et rursus: Nuntii mortis, ira regis. Interrogavit sapientes, qui ex more regio ei semper aderant. Nam et Philosophus docet, quod rex seu princeps debet sibi associare multos sapientes, ut habeat quasi oculos multos, quorum directione juvetur: quia plus vident oculi multi, quam unus. Et sic fecit Assuerus. Nam additur: et illorum faciebat cuncta consilio, scientium leges ac jura majorum, id est instituta a sapientioribus et supremis principibus. Erant autem primi et proximi septem duces Persarum atque Medorum. Talibus committenda est gubernatio subditorum, videlicet peritis et expertis in omnibus, qui quærant bonum commune, non propria commoda, et justi sint ac prudentes. Et quamvis rex fuit iratus, non tamen sine horum consilio voluit ad ultionem procedere, quia ira oculum cordis excæcat. Propter quod Seneca: Nihil (inquit) volo tibi irascenti licere, quoniam tibi irato omnia licita esse videntur, quæ scilicet ira persuadet. Qui videbant faciem regis, id est, familiariores ei fuerunt et magis contubernales, et primi post eum residere soliti erant, sive in eadem, sive in alia mensa, et in consiliis et consimilibus causis. Cui sententiæ Vasthi regina subjaceret.
paras.en: [[1:12|Whereupon the king, being angry, and inflamed with a very great fury|Unde iratus rex, et nimio furore succensus]]. Now the anger of kings is to be avoided, as far as can reasonably be done; for, as Solomon says in the Proverbs: [[Prov 19:12|As the roaring of a lion, so also is the anger of a king|Sicut fremitus leonis, ita et ira regis]]: [[Prov 20:2|he that provoketh him, sinneth against his own soul|qui provocat eum, peccat in animam suam]]. And again: The wrath of a king is as [[Prov 16:14|messengers of death|Nuntii mortis]]. [[1:13|Asked the wise men, who according to the custom of the kings, were always near his person|Interrogavit sapientes, qui ex more regio ei semper aderant]]. For the Philosopher too teaches that a king or prince ought to take many wise men to himself, so as to have as it were many eyes, by whose guidance he may be helped; for many eyes see more than one. And so did Assuerus, for it is added: [[1:13|and all he did was by their counsel, who knew the laws, and judgments of their forefathers|et illorum faciebat cuncta consilio, scientium leges ac jura majorum]], that is, the things laid down by wiser men and by the highest princes. [[1:14|Now the chief and nearest him were|Erant autem primi et proximi]] … [[1:14|seven princes of the Persians and of the Medes|septem duces Persarum atque Medorum]]. To such men the government of subjects is to be committed: to those skilled and experienced in all things, who seek the common good, not their own advantage, and who are just and prudent. And although the king was angry, he would not proceed to vengeance without their counsel, for anger blinds the eye of the heart. Hence Seneca says: I will have nothing allowed thee while thou art angry, since to thee in thy anger all things seem lawful, namely, those that anger urges. [[1:14|who saw the face of the king|Qui videbant faciem regis]], that is, who were more familiar with him and more his companions, [[1:14|and were used to sit first after him|et primi post eum residere soliti erant]], whether at the same table or at another, and in councils and such matters: [[1:15|What sentence ought to pass upon Vasthi the queen|Cui sententiæ Vasthi regina subjaceret]].

paras.t: Responditque Mamuchan, qui inter septem sapientes in littera ultimo ponitur, audiente rege atque principibus: Non solum regem læsit regina, derogando regis honori, et hoc publice coram cunctis: per quod scandalizavit quamplurimos, et ejus exemplo feminæ spernent maritorum suorum præcepta, nisi ipsa tam acriter puniatur, quod ceteræ matronæ inde terreantur, et a consimili compescantur. Et hoc est quod prolixe narratur in textu qui planus est. Placuit consilium ejus, id est eunuchi istius, regi et principibus, ut scilicet regina Vasthi ultra non ingrederetur ad regem, sed regnum illius, id est communionem in regno convenientem uxori regis, altera quæ melior est illa, accipiat, et cunctæ uxores deferant maritis suis honorem. Hinc rex omnibus suis provinciis scripsit, viros esse principes ac majores in domibus suis.
paras.en: [[1:16|And Mamuchan answered|Responditque Mamuchan]], who is put last among the seven wise men in the letter, [[1:16|in the hearing of the king and the princes|audiente rege atque principibus]]: [[1:16|Queen Vasthi hath not only injured the king|Non solum regem læsit regina]], by detracting from the king's honour, and that publicly before all: by which she has scandalized very many, and by her example women will spurn the commands of their husbands, unless she is punished so sharply that the other matrons are frightened by it and restrained from the like. And this is what is told at length in the text, which is plain. [[1:21|His counsel pleased the king, and the princes|Placuit consilium ejus regi et principibus]] (*his*, that is, of this eunuch [Denis takes Mamuchan for one of the eunuchs]), namely [[1:19|that Vasthi come in no more to the king|regina Vasthi ultra non ingrederetur ad regem]], [[1:19|but another, that is better than her, be made queen in her place|sed regnum illius altera, quæ melior est illa, accipiat]] [literally, “that another, who is better than she, receive her kingdom”], that is, the share in the kingdom that befits the king's wife, [[1:20|and let all wives, as well of the greater as of the lesser, give honour to their husbands|et cunctæ uxores deferant maritis suis honorem]]. Hence the king wrote to all his provinces [[1:22|that the husbands should be rulers and masters in their houses|viros esse principes ac majores in domibus suis]].

paras.t: Unde et juxta Apostolica documenta, vir caput est mulieris. Et viri est, instruere ac dirigere conjugem in agendis, ac errantem corripere. Hinc in Genesi legitur dictum primæ mulieri a Domino: Sub viri potestate eris, et ipse dominabitur tui. Ideo et beatissimus princeps apostolici chori, in prima sua Canonica ait: Similiter mulieres subditæ sint viris suis, sicut Sara obediebat Abrahæ, dominum eum vocans. Verumtamen principatus viri in uxorem, non est per omnia, sicut principatus domini ad servum, ut etiam docet Philosophus: imo in multis ad paria judicantur. Sed in principalibus et arduis rebus ac causis, vir principalior est: nam et sexus femineus est sexus subjectionis. Et communiter viri in naturalibus et judicio rationis atque constantia cordis, perfectiores sunt feminis, quamvis interdum contingat oppositum.
paras.en: Hence too, according to the teaching of the Apostle, [[Eph 5:23|the husband is the head of the wife|vir caput est mulieris]][[1 Cor 11:3||]]. And it is the husband's part to instruct and direct his wife in what is to be done, and to correct her when she errs. Hence we read in Genesis that it was said to the first woman by the Lord: [[Gen 3:16|thou shalt be under thy husband's power, and he shall have dominion over thee|Sub viri potestate eris, et ipse dominabitur tui]]. Therefore the most blessed prince of the apostolic choir too says in his first Canonical Epistle: [[1 Pet 3:1|In like manner also, let wives be subject to their husbands|Similiter mulieres subditæ sint viris suis]], [[1 Pet 3:6|As Sara obeyed Abraham, calling him lord|sicut Sara obediebat Abrahæ, dominum eum vocans]][[Gen 18:12||]] [the margin gives Gen. xvi (read xviii?), 12, where Sara calls Abraham her lord]. Yet the rule of a husband over his wife is not in all things like the rule of a master over a servant, as the Philosopher also teaches; indeed in many things they are judged as equals. But in the chief and weighty matters and causes the husband is the more principal; for the female sex is the sex of subjection. And commonly men are more perfect than women in natural gifts, in the judgement of reason and in steadfastness of heart, though sometimes the opposite happens.

paras.t: Postremo quidam spiritualizant istam historiam, intelligentes Christum per Assuerum: de qua expositione supersedere melius puto.
paras.en: Lastly, some give this history a spiritual sense, understanding Christ by Assuerus; but I think it better to refrain from that exposition.

2.title: Expositio capituli secundi: His itaque gestis postquam regis Assueri indignatio deferbuerat
2.title_en: Exposition of the second chapter: After this, when the wrath of king Assuerus was appeased

paras.t: Hic describitur qualiter Esther facta est conjux regis.
paras.en: Here it is described how Esther became the king's wife.

paras.t: His itaque gestis postquam regis Assueri indignatio deferbuerat, id est, fervere desiit, et mitescere cœpit cor ejus circa abjectam uxorem. Ira enim, sicut et ceteræ passiones appetitus sensitivi, fit cum corporali transmutatione: qua sedata, sedatur et passio, saltem a vehementia sua. Et specialiter generatur cum sanguinis ebullitione, fellis evaporatione, inflammationeque choleræ: quibus cessantibus, ira mitescit. Recordatus est Vasthi, prioris uxoris, et quæ fecisset, id est inobedientiam ejus, et quæ passa esset, videlicet libellum repudii seu repudiationem: et cœpit in corde suo ejus inobedientiam quodammodo excusare, propter causam in præcedenti articulo introductam. Sicque apparuit ei, quod ultra condignum esset punita: quod non videbatur regiam decere majestatem, ad quam constat præcipue spectare clementiam, juxta illud Proverbiorum, Roboratur clementia thronus regis. Quamvis autem in præcedenti capitulo dictum sit, quod regi Assuero placuit eunuchi consilium de Vasthi abjectione, Josephus tamen undecimo Antiquitatum libro enarrat, quod consilium eunuchi rex graviter tulit, detentus amore uxoris, et reminiscens ipsius decorem, et tristabatur quod propter irrevocabile suum edictum eam non potuit revocare. Idcirco in sollicitudinibus et mœrore permansit. Quem videntes amici nimio mœrore confectum, persuadebant ut amorem pristinæ conjugis et amorem nil profuturum deponeret, et quæreret per universam terram virgines decoras, ex quibus pulchriorem haberet uxorem, arbitrantes sic posse exstingui prioris cupidinem, alia introducta, et desiderium a muliere projecta subtractum, paulatim posse ad cohabitantem converti. Hoc est ergo quod subditur.
paras.en: [[2:1|After this, when the wrath of king Assuerus was appeased|His itaque gestis postquam regis Assueri indignatio deferbuerat]] [*deferbuerat*, literally “had stopped boiling”], that is, ceased to boil, and his heart began to grow mild towards the wife he had put away. For anger, like the other passions of the sensitive appetite, comes with a bodily change; and when that is calmed, the passion too is calmed, at least from its vehemence. And in particular it is produced with the boiling of the blood, the vapours of the gall and the inflaming of the choler; and when these cease, anger grows mild. [[2:1|he remembered Vasthi|Recordatus est Vasthi]], his former wife, [[2:1|and what she had done|et quæ fecisset]], that is, her disobedience, [[2:1|and what she had suffered|et quæ passa esset]], namely the bill of divorce or repudiation; and he began in his heart in some way to excuse her disobedience, for the reason brought in in the preceding article. And so it seemed to him that she had been punished beyond her desert, which did not seem to befit the royal majesty, to which clemency is known to belong above all, according to the word of the Proverbs: [[Prov 20:28|his throne is strengthened by clemency|Roboratur clementia thronus regis]] [the margin gives Prov. xx, 28]. Now although it was said in the preceding chapter that the eunuch's counsel about putting away Vasthi pleased King Assuerus, Josephus nevertheless relates in the eleventh book of the Antiquities that the king took the eunuch's counsel hard, being held by love of his wife; and remembering her beauty he grieved that because of his irrevocable edict he could not call her back. So he remained in cares and sorrow. His friends, seeing him worn with too much grief, urged him to put away the love of his former wife, a love that would profit him nothing, and to seek through the whole land for comely virgins, from whom he might have a more beautiful wife; thinking that so the longing for the first might be quenched when another was brought in, and that the desire, withdrawn from the woman cast off, might little by little be turned to the one living with him. This, then, is what is added.

paras.t: Dixeruntque pueri, id est familiares et cari, regis, atque ministri domestici sive præcipui: Quærantur regi puellæ virgines speciosæ, et tradantur in domo feminarum, ad usum regis deputatarum, sub manu Egei eunuchi. Eunuchus in Scripturis quandoque accipitur pro castrato: et sic videtur hic accipi. Interdum vero, pro continente et probo in moribus: sicque sumitur præcedenti capitulo, quum dicuntur septem eunuchi in conspectu regis ministrasse. Qui est præpositus et custos mulierum regiarum, quæ usui regis deputantur: quibus ille eunuchus habuit providere de ornatu et victu atque custodia; et accipiant mundum muliebrem, id est apparatum ad ornatum et corporis mundificationem pertinentem, et cetera ad usus feminarum ac cultum earum, necessaria. Et quæcumque inter omnes oculis regis placuerit præ ceteris, ipsa regnet pro Vasthi. Placuit sermo regi; et ita ut suggesserant, jussit fieri.
paras.en: [[2:2|And the king's servants|Dixeruntque pueri]], that is, his familiar and dear servants, [[2:2|and his officers said|atque ministri]], those of his household or his chief ones: [[2:2|Let young women be sought for the king, virgins and beautiful|Quærantur regi puellæ virgines speciosæ]], [[2:3|and put them into the house of the women|et tradantur in domo feminarum]] set apart for the king's use, [[2:3|under the hand of Egeus the eunuch|sub manu Egei eunuchi]]. *Eunuch* in the Scriptures is sometimes taken for a castrated man, and so it seems to be taken here; but sometimes for a man continent and upright in conduct, and so it is taken in the preceding chapter, when seven eunuchs are said to have served in the king's presence[[Esth 1:10||]] [the margin gives Esther i, 10]. [[2:3|who is the overseer and keeper of the king's women|Qui est præpositus et custos mulierum regiarum]], who are set apart for the king's use, and for whom that eunuch had to provide adornment, food and guard; [[2:3|and let them receive women's ornaments|et accipiant mundum muliebrem]], that is, the apparatus belonging to adornment and the cleansing of the body, [[2:3|and other things necessary for their use|et cetera ad usus necessaria]], that is, for the use and adornment of the women. [[2:4|And whosoever among them all shall please the king's eyes|Et quæcumque inter omnes oculis regis placuerit]] above the rest, [[2:4|let her be queen instead of Vasthi. The word pleased the king: and he commanded it should be done as they had suggested|ipsa regnet pro Vasthi. Placuit sermo regi; et ita ut suggesserant, jussit fieri]].

paras.t: Erat autem vir Judæus in Susis civitate, vocabulo Mardochæus, de stirpe Jemini; de qua et Saul primo Regum fuisse asseritur; qui translatus fuerat: hoc præcedenti articulo expositum est: nutricius Esther, quam defunctis Esther parentibus, adoptavit in filiam: nam filia fuit fratris sui. Esther, inter ceteras puellas tradita eunucho. Secundum Josephum, de Babylonia fuit adducta, et Mardochæus ejus amore secutus est eam, et sic habitavit in Susis.
paras.en: [[2:5|There was a man in the city of Susan, a Jew, named Mardochai|Erat autem vir Judæus in Susis civitate, vocabulo Mardochæus]], [[2:5|of the race of Jemini|de stirpe Jemini]], of which Saul too is said in the first book of Kings to have been[[1 Kings 9:1||]] [the margin gives I Reg. ix, 1]; [[2:6|Who had been carried away|qui translatus fuerat]]: this was explained in the preceding article; [[2:7|And he had brought up|nutricius]] [*nutricius*, “foster-father”] Esther; [[2:7|her father and mother being dead|defunctis Esther parentibus]], he [[2:7|adopted her for his daughter|adoptavit in filiam]]: for she was his brother's daughter. [[2:8|Esther also among the rest of the maidens was delivered|Esther, inter ceteras puellas tradita]] to the eunuch. According to Josephus she was brought from Babylon, and Mardochai followed her out of love for her, and so came to live in Susan.

paras.t: Quæ placuit ei, puta eunucho, et acceleraret mundum muliebrem, id est, mox festinavit eam ornare, habens spem firmam, quod rex eam eligeret in uxorem. Nam, ut Josephus contestatur, gratia vultus sui respicientium delectabat magis adspectum. Et traderet ei partes suas, id est ea quæ ad ejus pertinebant decorationem, et septem puellas speciosissimas, id est valde pulchras, minus tamen quam Esther; et tam ipsam quam ejus pedissequas ornaret atque excoleret, id est, valde exquisite componeret, cupiens ejus promotionem, et ut ipse per hoc consequeretur favorem illius. Quæ noluit ei indicare populum et patriam suam. Mardochæus enim præceperat ei, ut de hac re omnino reticeret. Judæi quippe tunc erant ibi captivi, et a multis contempti, ac singularis religionis.
paras.en: [[2:9|And she pleased him|Quæ placuit ei]], namely the eunuch, [[2:9|to hasten the women's ornaments|et acceleraret mundum muliebrem]], that is, he made haste at once to adorn her, having a firm hope that the king would choose her as his wife. For, as Josephus testifies, by the grace of her face she delighted the eyes of those who looked on her more than the others did. [[2:9|and to deliver to her her part|Et traderet ei partes suas]], that is, what belonged to her adornment, [[2:9|and seven of the most beautiful maidens|et septem puellas speciosissimas]], that is, very beautiful, yet less so than Esther; [[2:9|and to adorn and deck out both her and her waiting maids|et tam ipsam quam ejus pedissequas ornaret atque excoleret]] [the print is damaged here; the words are read with the help of the Vulgate], that is, to set them out most exquisitely, desiring her advancement, and that he himself might gain her favour by this. [[2:10|And she would not tell him her people nor her country|Quæ noluit ei indicare populum et patriam suam]]. [[2:10|For Mardochai had charged her to say nothing at all of that|Mardochæus enim præceperat ei, ut de hac re omnino reticeret]]. For the Jews were then captives there, despised by many, and of a peculiar religion.

paras.t: Quum autem venisset tempus singularum per ordinem puellarum, ut intrarent ad regem. Ad quiescendum cum illo, intrabant successive, seu quælibet die suo. Unde Josephus ait: Per singulos dies ad concubitum unam regi mittebat. Expletis omnibus quæ ad cultum muliebrem pertinebant, scilicet in balneationibus, unctionibus, aromatumque applicationibus et vestimentorum decore, mensis duodecimus vertebatur: quia per integrum annum præparabantur ad regis conjunctionem; ita dumtaxat, ut sex mensibus ungerentur oleo myrtino, id est humore, gutta seu lacrima fluente de arbore quæ myrtus vocatur, cujus oleum carnem mundificat, et aliis sex mensibus quibusdam pigmentis, id est confectionibus, et aromatibus uterentur, ad reddendum corpus feminæ magis suave et molle ad tactum, ne quid inconvenientis odoris inveniretur in aliqua. Ingredientesque ad regem de die in palatium quidquid postulassent ad ornatum pertinens, accipiebant ab aliquo a rege ad hoc deputato; et ut eis placuerat, compositæ, id est ad proprium libitum exculte et decoratæ, de triclinio, id est aula seu palatio feminarum, ad regis cubiculum transibant. Et quæ intrabat vespere, egrediebatur mane, atque inde in secundas ædes, id est mansiones, deducebatur, quæ sub manu Susagari eunuchi erant, qui concubinis regis præsidebat. Aliqui opinantur, quod rex universas puellas secum dormientes duxit uxores, et tamen concubinæ vocentur, tanquam conjuges secundariæ, minusque principales, sicut in Genesi Zelpha et Bala quandoque vocantur uxores Jacob, aliquando concubinæ. Alii magis tenent oppositum. Nam et gentiles pro magna parte, concubitum simplicis fornicationis non reputabant peccatum: imo, ut dictum est in libro Judith, fœdum fuit apud Assyrios, ut femina irrideat virum, agendo ut immunis transeat ab eo.
paras.en: [[2:12|Now when every virgin's turn came to go in to the king|Quum autem venisset tempus singularum per ordinem puellarum, ut intrarent ad regem]], to rest with him, they went in one after another, each on her own day. Hence Josephus says: Every day he sent one to the king to lie with him. [[2:12|after all had been done for setting them off to advantage|Expletis omnibus quæ ad cultum muliebrem pertinebant]], namely in bathings, anointings, the applying of spices and the beauty of garments, [[2:12|it was the twelfth month|mensis duodecimus vertebatur]]: for they were prepared for a whole year for union with the king; [[2:12|so that for six months they were anointed with oil of myrrh|ita dumtaxat, ut sex mensibus ungerentur oleo myrtino]] [Denis reads *myrtino*, “of myrtle”, for the Vulgate's *myrrhino*], that is, with the moisture, drop or tear flowing from the tree called myrtle, whose oil cleanses the flesh, [[2:12|and for other six months they used certain perfumes|et aliis sex mensibus quibusdam pigmentis]], that is, confections, [[2:12|and sweet spices|et aromatibus uterentur]], to make the woman's body sweeter and softer to the touch, so that no unseemly smell might be found in any of them. [[2:13|And when they were going in to the king, whatsoever they asked to adorn themselves they received|Ingredientesque ad regem, quidquid postulassent ad ornatum pertinens, accipiebant]] (going in to the palace by day) from someone appointed by the king for this; [[2:13|and being decked out, as it pleased them|et ut eis placuerat, compositæ]], that is, adorned and decked out at their own pleasure, [[2:13|they passed from the chamber of the women to the king's chamber|de triclinio feminarum ad regis cubiculum transibant]] (*triclinium*, that is, the hall or palace of the women). [[2:14|And she that went in at evening, came out in the morning, and from thence she was conducted to the second house|Et quæ intrabat vespere, egrediebatur mane, atque inde in secundas ædes]], that is, dwellings, [[2:14|that was under the hand of Susagaz the eunuch, who had the charge over the king's concubines|quæ sub manu Susagari eunuchi erant, qui concubinis regis præsidebat]]. Some think that the king took as wives all the maidens who slept with him, and yet they are called concubines, as secondary and less principal wives, as in Genesis Zelpha and Bala are sometimes called the wives of Jacob[[Gen 30:4||]], sometimes his concubines[[Gen 35:22||]] [the margin gives Gen. xxx and, partly unreadable, xxxv]. Others rather hold the opposite. For the Gentiles for the most part did not count lying in simple fornication a sin; indeed, as was said in the book of Judith, [[Jdt 12:11|it is looked upon as shameful among the Assyrians, if a woman mock a man, by doing so as to pass free from him|fœdum fuit apud Assyrios, ut femina irrideat virum, agendo ut immunis transeat ab eo]].

paras.t: Evoluto autem tempore, instabat dies quo Esther intrare debebat ad regem. Quæ non quæsivit muliebrem cultum. Non enim aspirabat ad regis complacentiam atque conjugium, ut infra patebit: ideo commisit ornatum suum eunucho. Hinc subditur: Sed quæcumque voluit Egeus eunuchus, hæc ei ad ornatum dedit. Erat enim formosa valde et incredibili pulchritudine, omniumque oculis gratiosa et amabilis videbatur: quod totum ex divina providentia factum est, ut per eam populus Israel liberaretur. Ecce qualis artifex est omnipotens Deus, et quam pulcher, pulcherrimus, incomparabiliter pulcher et superpulcherrimus, atque ad intuendum superdeliciosissimus, infiniteque gratiosus, superamabilis est ille in semetipso, et ad fruendum superdulcissimus, qui in tam modica corporis parte, in fragili vasculo, in mortali materia vilique gleba tantam pulchritudinem, amabilitatem et delectabilitatem constituit. Denique pulchritudinem illam corporalem mirabiliter venustavit et auxit supernaturalis pulchritudo mentis in donis gratiæ ac virtutum, redundans ac resplendens in corpore; pulchritudo quoque moralis, in venustissimis moribus, apparatu et compositione exteriori consistens.
paras.en: [[2:15|And as the time came orderly about, the day was at hand|Evoluto autem tempore, instabat dies]], [[2:15|when Esther|quo Esther]] … [[2:15|was to go in to the king|intrare debebat ad regem]]. [[2:15|But she sought not women's ornaments|Quæ non quæsivit muliebrem cultum]]. For she did not aspire to please the king and to marry him, as will appear below; and so she left her adornment to the eunuch. Hence it is added: [[2:15|but whatsoever Egeus the eunuch|Sed quæcumque voluit Egeus eunuchus]] … [[2:15|had a mind, he gave her to adorn her|hæc ei ad ornatum dedit]]. [[2:15|For she was exceeding fair, and her incredible beauty made her appear agreeable and amiable in the eyes of all|Erat enim formosa valde et incredibili pulchritudine, omniumque oculis gratiosa et amabilis videbatur]]: all of which was done by divine providence, so that the people of Israel might be delivered through her. Behold what an artist almighty God is, and how beautiful, most beautiful, incomparably beautiful and more than most beautiful, more than most delightful to behold, infinitely gracious and more than lovable he is in himself, and more than most sweet to enjoy, who in so small a part of the body, in a frail vessel, in mortal matter and a lowly clod, has set so great a beauty, loveliness and delightfulness. Moreover, that bodily beauty was wonderfully graced and increased by the supernatural beauty of the mind in the gifts of grace and of the virtues, overflowing and shining out in the body; and also by moral beauty, which lies in the most graceful manners, bearing and outward composure.

paras.t: Ducta est itaque ad cubiculum regis mense decimo, qui vocatur Tebeth, id est Januarius apud nos: non utique decimo mense suæ expolitionis et præparationis ad regis accessum; sed decimo mense septimi anni regni Assueri. Et adamavit eam rex plus quam omnes mulieres, vel divisim vel conjunctim acceptas, loquendo de maritali affectu. Et quia tantam virtuositatem, pudorem et honestatem consideravit in puella, posuit diadema regni in capite ejus, fecitque eam regnare loco Vasthi. Et jussit convivium præparari permagnificum cunctis principibus et servis suis, quod secundum Josephum, Scholasticamque historiam, duravit per integrum mensem. Et dedit requiem in universis provinciis, id est, a subditis suis non exegit solita tributa sive obsequia anno illo aut circiter. Vel sensus est, quod fecit eos ad tempus a manualibus cessare laboribus, puta per mensem, quum Josephus dicat, quod præcepit eis festa pro suis nuptiis celebrare. Ac dona largitus est suis officiatis, cognatis, amicis, domesticis, juxta magnificentiam principalem, id est regalem et imperialem, videlicet liberaliter valde. Quod est contra præsidentes, qui in nuptiis suis aut sobolis suæ, gravant subditos suos exactionibus seu munerum exhibitionibus quas requirunt.
paras.en: [[2:16|So she was brought to the chamber|Ducta est itaque ad cubiculum regis]] of the king [[2:16|the tenth month, which is called Tebeth|mense decimo, qui vocatur Tebeth]], that is, our January: not, indeed, the tenth month of her adorning and preparation for going in to the king, but the tenth month of the seventh year of the reign of Assuerus. [[2:17|And the king loved her more than all the women|Et adamavit eam rex plus quam omnes mulieres]], whether taken one by one or all together, speaking of a husband's love. And because he saw such virtue, modesty and seemliness in the maiden, [[2:17|he set the royal crown on her head, and made her queen instead of Vasthi|posuit diadema regni in capite ejus, fecitque eam regnare loco Vasthi]]. [[2:18|And he commanded a magnificent feast to be prepared for all the princes, and for his servants|Et jussit convivium præparari permagnificum cunctis principibus et servis suis]], which according to Josephus and the Scholastic History lasted a whole month. [[2:18|And he gave rest to all the provinces|Et dedit requiem in universis provinciis]], that is, he did not exact from his subjects the usual tributes or services for that year or thereabouts. Or the sense is that he made them cease from manual labour for a time, say for a month, since Josephus says that he commanded them to keep festival for his wedding. [[2:18|and bestowed gifts|Ac dona largitus est]] on his officers, kinsmen, friends and household, [[2:18|according to princely magnificence|juxta magnificentiam principalem]], that is, royal and imperial, namely very liberally. This is against those rulers who at their own weddings or their children's burden their subjects with exactions, or with the presents they require of them.

paras.t: Quumque secundo quærerentur virgines et congregarentur, Mardochæus manebat ad januam regis. Cur jam post initum cum Esther connubium, virgines quærebantur? Putant quidam, quod ad concubinatum; alii dicunt quod ipsa Esther nequaquam volente prodere genealogiam suam, rex simulavit se velle ducere aliam, et simulatorie fecit virgines quæri, quatenus sic extorqueret a conjuge genus ipsius. Ad quod referunt quod sequitur. Necdum prodiderat, id est manifestaverat, Esther patriam et populum suum, juxta mandatum ejus, id est Mardochæi. Quidquid enim ille præcipiebat, observabat Esther, et ita cuncta faciebat, ut eo tempore solita erat, quo eam parvulam nutriebat: in quo patent humilitas et obedientia Esther. Quidam vero paululum promoti, mox intumescunt, et obedire despiciunt suis parentibus aut magistris, seu his a quibus sunt instituti.
paras.en: [[2:19|And when the virgins were sought the second time, and gathered together, Mardochai stayed at the king's gate|Quumque secundo quærerentur virgines et congregarentur, Mardochæus manebat ad januam regis]] [the print is damaged here; the words are read with the help of the Vulgate]. Why were virgins sought now, after the marriage with Esther had been made? Some think it was for concubinage; others say that, since Esther would by no means disclose her descent, the king pretended that he wished to marry another, and had virgins sought by way of pretence, so as to wring from his wife her race. To this they refer what follows: [[2:20|Neither had Esther as yet declared|Necdum prodiderat]], that is, made known, [[2:20|her country and people, according to his commandment|Esther patriam et populum suum, juxta mandatum ejus]], that is, Mardochai's. [[2:20|For whatsoever he commanded, Esther observed: and she did all things in the same manner as she was wont at that time when he brought her up a little one|Quidquid enim ille præcipiebat, observabat Esther, et ita cuncta faciebat, ut eo tempore solita erat, quo eam parvulam nutriebat]]: in which the humility and obedience of Esther are plain. But some, when they are a little advanced, at once swell up, and scorn to obey their parents or masters, or those by whom they were brought up.

paras.t: Eo igitur tempore quo Mardochæus ad januam regis morabatur, irati sunt duo eunuchi regis, volueruntque insurgere in regem, et occidere eum. Cujus rei causa nescitur, nisi quod servi sæpe ex indignatione, ambitione, traditione machinantur in mortem principis sui, quemadmodum patet tertio et quarto Regum, ubi reges Israel a servis suis occisi leguntur. Quod Mardochæum non latuit. Dicunt nonnulli, quod eunuchi audiente Mardochæo, contulerunt de regis interfectione in lingua quam putabant non intelligere Mardochæum. Josephus vero dicit, quod unus eunuchorum habuit servum Judæum, cognoscentem domini sui insidias, et retulit Mardochæo. Statimque nuntiavit reginæ Esther, et illa regi ex nomine Mardochæi. Quæsitum est, et inventum; et appensus est uterque in patibulo. Et ita rex sapienter processit, non statim incaute credendo, sed examinando negotium. Et jussit rex ut in libro memoriali scriberetur, ut pro vita sua aliquid repensaret ei. Mandatumque est historiis, id est in libris historialibus scriptum, et annalibus traditum coram rege. Annales vocantur libri historici, in quibus scribuntur quæ singulis annis contingunt sub regibus, ut reges talia recolendo, ex memoria præteritorum caute se habeant per considerationem præsentium, ac providentiam futurorum.
paras.en: [[2:21|At that time, therefore, when Mardochai abode at the king's gate|Eo igitur tempore quo Mardochæus ad januam regis morabatur]], [[2:21|two of the king's eunuchs|duo eunuchi regis]] [[2:21|were angry|irati sunt]], [[2:21|and they designed to rise up against the king, and to kill him|volueruntque insurgere in regem, et occidere eum]]. The cause of this is not known, except that servants often plot the death of their prince out of indignation, ambition or treachery, as is plain in the third and fourth books of Kings, where kings of Israel are read to have been killed by their servants[[3 Kings 15:27||]][[3 Kings 16:9||]][[4 Kings 15:10||]] [the margin, partly unreadable, gives III Reg. xv, 27–29; xvi, 9–11; IV Reg. xv, 10, 14, 25, 30]. [[2:22|And Mardochai had notice of it|Quod Mardochæum non latuit]]. Some say that the eunuchs spoke of killing the king in Mardochai's hearing, in a language they thought Mardochai did not understand. But Josephus says that one of the eunuchs had a Jewish servant who knew of his master's plot and told it to Mardochai. [[2:22|and immediately he told it to queen Esther: and she to the king in Mardochai's name|Statimque nuntiavit reginæ Esther, et illa regi ex nomine Mardochæi]]. [[2:23|It was inquired into, and found out: and they were both hanged on a gibbet|Quæsitum est, et inventum; et appensus est uterque in patibulo]]. And so the king proceeded wisely, not believing at once and rashly, but examining the matter. And the king commanded that it be written in the book of records, so that he might make him some return for his life. [[2:23|And it was put in the histories|Mandatumque est historiis]], that is, written in the books of history, [[2:23|and recorded in the chronicles before the king|et annalibus traditum coram rege]]. The books of history are called annals, in which are written what happens each year under the kings, so that the kings, recalling such things, may conduct themselves warily from the memory of the past, by consideration of the present and foresight of the future.

paras.t: Circa capitulum istud aliqua possent inquiri: an scilicet regi licuit suam sic abjicere conjugem, quum inseparabilitas dicatur esse de ratione matrimonii; et an illa repudiata atque vivente, licuit ei ducere aliam. Item, an licuit ipsi Esther cum rege gentili contrahere, quum hoc fuerit prohibitum lege; et an fuerit vera uxor regis, quum dispar cultus impediat matrimonium contrahendum, dirimatque contractum. Ad quæ longum est plenarie respondere. Breviter autem tangendo dici potest, non oportere Assuerum excusare a culpa: ipsamque Esther ex divina præordinatione ac dispensatione contraxisse cum illo, sicut Samson cum Philistæa, ut patet in libro Judicum, ubi habetur, quod res illa agebatur a Domino: et Salomon adhuc bonus cum filia Pharaonis, ut patet tertio Regum. Horum autem magistralis discussio, ad quartum spectat Sententiarum.
paras.en: Some things could be asked about this chapter: namely, whether it was lawful for the king to put away his wife so, since inseparability is said to belong to the nature of marriage; and whether, she being put away and still alive, it was lawful for him to marry another. Again, whether it was lawful for Esther to contract marriage with a Gentile king, since this was forbidden by the law[[Deut 7:3||]] [the margin gives Deut. vii, 3]; and whether she was truly the king's wife, since disparity of worship hinders the contracting of marriage, and annuls it when contracted. To answer these fully would be long. But touching on them briefly, it can be said that there is no need to excuse Assuerus from fault, and that Esther contracted marriage with him by divine preordaining and dispensation, as Samson did with the Philistine woman, as is plain in the book of Judges, where it is said that [[Judg 14:4|the thing was done by the Lord|res illa agebatur a Domino]]; and Solomon, while still good, with the daughter of Pharao, as is plain in the third book of Kings[[3 Kings 3:1||]]. The masterly discussion of these things belongs to the fourth book of the Sentences.

3.title: Elucidatio capituli tertii: Post hæc rex Assuerus exaltavit Aman
3.title_en: Explanation of the third chapter: After these things king Assuerus advanced Aman

paras.t: Capitulo isto describitur, qualiter Aman exaltatus a rege, procuravit ab eodem populum Judæorum morti adjudicari.
paras.en: This chapter describes how Aman, advanced by the king, procured from him that the people of the Jews be sentenced to death.

paras.t: Post hæc rex Assuerus exaltavit Aman filium Amadathi, qui erat de stirpe Agag regis Amalecitarum: quos Saul vastavit, et quorum regem jam nominatum, Samuel propheta concidit in frusta, ut primo Regum libro legitur; et posuit solium ejus super omnes principes, quos habebat, id est super ceteros, qui sub ipso rege præerant populo, sicut Pharao exaltavit electum Joseph. Et sic Aman fuit primus post regem. Verumtamen infra legitur, quod Aman fuit animo et gente seu genere Macedo. Ex quo apparet, quod non fuit Amalecites. Ad quod respondebitur ibi.
paras.en: [[3:1|After these things, king Assuerus advanced Aman, the son of Amadathi, who was of the race of Agag|Post hæc rex Assuerus exaltavit Aman filium Amadathi, qui erat de stirpe Agag]], king of the Amalecites, whom Saul laid waste[[1 Kings 15:7||]], and whose king just named the prophet Samuel hewed in pieces, as is read in the first book of Kings[[1 Kings 15:33||]] [the margin's numeral reads "I Reg. xx"; the passage is 1 Kings 15:33]; [[3:1|and he set his throne above all the princes that were with him|et posuit solium ejus super omnes principes, quos habebat]], that is, above the others who governed the people under the king himself, as Pharao advanced the chosen Joseph[[Gen 41:40||]] [the margin note here is unreadable; the story is Gen 41:40–43]. And so Aman was the first after the king. Yet it is read further on that Aman was a Macedonian in mind and in nation, or race[[Esth 16:10||]]. From which it appears that he was not an Amalecite. This will be answered there.

paras.t: Cunctique servi regis flectebant genu, et adorabant Aman. Sic enim jusserat eis imperator. Solus Mardochæus non flectebat genu, ad reverentiam Aman, neque adorabat eum, ne honorem Deo debitum homini exhiberet: quia ut dicitur, Aman superbissimus voluit sibi non solum duliæ, sed et latriæ adorationem impendi. Siquidem cultus duliæ poterat ei exhiberi, tanquam personæ excellenti in officio regiminis constitutæ. Aman autem super hominem impiissime se extollens, voluit adorari ut Deus: quemadmodum Nabuchodonosor rex Assyriorum, videlicet Cambyses, et Caius imperator, ut legitur.
paras.en: [[3:2|And all the king's servants|Cunctique servi regis]] [[3:2|bent their knees, and worshipped Aman|flectebant genu, et adorabant Aman]]: [[3:2|for so the emperor had commanded them|Sic enim jusserat eis imperator]]: [[3:2|only Mardochai did not bend his knee|Solus Mardochæus non flectebat genu]] in reverence to Aman, [[3:2|nor worship him|neque adorabat eum]], lest he show to a man the honour due to God: because, as is said, the most proud Aman wished to have paid to himself not only the worship of dulia but also that of latria [dulia is the honour rightly given to creatures of excellence, latria the worship due to God alone]. For the reverence of dulia could have been shown him, as to a person of excellence set in the office of government. But Aman, most impiously exalting himself above man, wished to be worshipped as God: as did Nabuchodonosor king of the Assyrians, that is, Cambyses[[Jdt 3:13||]] [the margin note here is unreadable; Judith 3:13 is the likely passage], and the emperor Caius, as is read.

paras.t: Quod quum audisset, quod scilicet Mardochæus esset Judæus, nec se adoraret, iratus est valde. Oderat enim Judæos, a quibus cognovit progenitores et prædecessores suos fuisse occisos. Hinc servi regis annuntiaverunt ipsi Aman de Mardochæo, cupientes scire, an Mardochæus perseveraret in sententia, id est in responsione qua se dixit esse Judæum, et ideo non posse se hominem adorare. Et quoniam servi regis noverant Judæos esse exosos huic Aman, cupiebant scire ex quadam curiositate, an Mardochæus auderet hoc evidenter fateri, ipso Aman sciente aut audiente.
paras.en: [[3:5|Now when Aman had heard this|Quod quum audisset]], namely that Mardochai was a Jew and would not worship him, [[3:5|he was exceeding angry|iratus est valde]]. For he hated the Jews, by whom he knew that his forefathers and predecessors had been slain[[Ex 17:13||]][[1 Kings 15:8||]]. Hence the king's servants [[3:4|told Aman|annuntiaverunt ipsi Aman]] about Mardochai, [[3:4|desirous to know|cupientes scire]] whether Mardochai [[3:4|would continue in his resolution|perseveraret in sententia]], that is, in the answer by which he said that he was a Jew and therefore could not worship a man. And since the king's servants knew that the Jews were hateful to this Aman, they desired, out of a certain curiosity, to know whether Mardochai would dare to confess this openly, with Aman himself knowing or hearing it.

paras.t: Et pro nihilo duxit in unum, videlicet Mardochæum, mittere manus suas ultrices; magisque voluit omnem Judæorum perdere nationem, quæ erat in regno Assueri.
paras.en: [[3:6|And he counted it nothing|Et pro nihilo duxit]] against one, namely Mardochai, [[3:6|to lay his hands|mittere manus suas]] in vengeance; [[3:6|and he chose rather to destroy all the nation of the Jews that were in the kingdom of Assuerus|magisque voluit omnem Judæorum perdere nationem, quæ erat in regno Assueri]].

paras.t: Mense primo, cujus vocabulum est Nisan apud Judæos, et apud Latinos Aprilis, quamvis interdum concurrat partim cum Martio, missa est sors in urnam, quæ Hebraice dicitur Phur; id est, ipse Aman invidiosus sortilegus, misit sortem in vas quoddam, quod urna vocatur, ad sciendum per sortis oraculum, quo die mensis, et quo mense gens Judæorum deberet interfici; et exivit per sortis ostensionem mensis duodecimus, qui vocatur Adar secundum Hebræos, et Martius secundum Latinos. Exivit quoque per sortem tertiusdecimus dies mensis ejusdem.
paras.en: [[3:7|In the first month (which is called Nisan|Mense primo, cujus vocabulum est Nisan]] among the Jews, and April among the Latins, though at times it partly coincides with March, [[3:7|the lot was cast into an urn, which in Hebrew is called Phur|missa est sors in urnam, quæ Hebraice dicitur Phur]]: that is, Aman himself, an envious caster of lots, cast a lot into a certain vessel which is called an urn, to learn by the oracle of the lot [[3:7|on what day and what month the nation of the Jews should be destroyed|quo die mensis, et quo mense gens Judæorum deberet interfici]]; [[3:7|and there came out|et exivit]] by the showing of the lot [[3:7|the twelfth month, which is called Adar|mensis duodecimus, qui vocatur Adar]] according to the Hebrews, and March according to the Latins. There came out also by the lot the thirteenth day of the same month.

paras.t: Hæc fecit Aman ex vehementi indignatione et ira nequissima, tantam volens exercere vindictam in totum populum Judæorum, propter unius delictum, secundum suum judicium: quod tamen revera non fuit delictum, sed virtus. Superbi enim injuriam sibi factam, quamvis parvam, reputant valde gravem: idcirco in ulciscendo excedunt mensuram, et agunt contra justitiam. Denique, sciens se apud regem audientiam habere præcipuam, præsupponit se faciliter acquisiturum a rege judicium mortis contra Judæos.
paras.en: Aman did these things out of vehement indignation and most wicked anger, wishing to wreak so great a vengeance on the whole people of the Jews for the offence of one man, as he judged it: which in truth was no offence but virtue. For the proud reckon an injury done to them, however small, very grave; therefore in taking vengeance they exceed the measure, and act against justice. Lastly, knowing that he had a special hearing with the king, he takes for granted that he will easily obtain from the king a sentence of death against the Jews.

paras.t: Dixitque Aman regi: Est populus per omnes regni tui provincias dispersus, novis utens legibus et cerimoniis, colendo unum solum Deum, non deos, quos ab antiquis temporibus coluerunt gentiles. Nihilo minus lex Judæorum a tempore Moysis usque ad Assuerum perdurans, non fuit penitus nova, quamvis Aman sic dixerit ad inflammandum regem contra Judæos. Insuper et scita, id est decreta, regis contemnens. Unde dicitur plebiscitum. Et optime nosti quod non expediat regno tuo, scilicet bono communi et paci, ut insolescat, id est, contra solitum legum regni tui se habeat, per licentiam, id est permissionem manendi in vita et observantia sua.
paras.en: [[3:8|And Aman said|Dixitque Aman]] to the king: [[3:8|There is a people|Est populus]] [[3:8|scattered through all the provinces of thy kingdom|per omnes regni tui provincias dispersus]], [[3:8|that use new laws and ceremonies|novis utens legibus et cerimoniis]], by worshipping one God only, not the gods whom the gentiles worshipped from ancient times. Nevertheless the law of the Jews, which had lasted from the time of Moses down to Assuerus, was not new at all, though Aman spoke so to inflame the king against the Jews. [[3:8|and moreover despise the king's ordinances|Insuper et scita, id est decreta, regis contemnens]]: *ordinances* [*scita*], that is, decrees; whence the word *plebiscitum* [a decree of the people]. [[3:8|and thou knowest very well that it is not expedient for thy kingdom|Et optime nosti quod non expediat regno tuo]], that is, for the common good and peace, [[3:8|that they should grow insolent|ut insolescat]], that is, behave contrary to what is customary under the laws of thy kingdom, [[3:8|by impunity|per licentiam]] [*per licentiam*, literally "by licence"], that is, by being permitted to remain alive and keep their own observance.

paras.t: Si tibi placet, decerne, id est judica, ut pereat, id est occidatur, et decem millia talentorum appendam arcariis gazæ tuæ, id est custodibus thesaurorum tuorum. Hoc addidit Aman, ut videretur multum zelari pro rege et pro pace communi, cujus noverca et corruptrix solet esse dissimilitudo ac dispar cultus: et ne rex retraheretur a sententia mortis in Judæos dictanda, propter damnum tributorum quæ sibi a Judæis dabantur.
paras.en: [[3:9|If it please thee, decree|Si tibi placet, decerne]], that is, give judgment, [[3:9|that they may be destroyed|ut pereat]], that is, be put to death, [[3:9|and I will pay ten thousand talents to thy treasurers|et decem millia talentorum appendam arcariis gazæ tuæ]], that is, to the keepers of thy treasures. Aman added this so that he might seem very zealous for the king and for the common peace, whose stepmother and corrupter is wont to be unlikeness and diversity of worship; and lest the king be held back from pronouncing the sentence of death against the Jews by the loss of the tributes which the Jews paid him.
